items.desc: A natural gas utility in Vermont struck a first-in-the-nation deal that will soon be saving customers money by turning to geothermal energy. Vermont Gas launched the state’s “first community-scale geothermal project,” something the company’s CEO called one of the best solutions for lowering energy costs and one that many homeowners across the country hope to […] The post Geothermal Utilities Power
items.text:
A natural gas utility in Vermont struck a first-in-the-nation deal that will soon be saving customers money by turning to geothermal energy.
Vermont Gas launched the state’s “first community-scale geothermal project,” something the company’s CEO called one of the best solutions for lowering energy costs and one that many homeowners across the country hope to see in other areas.
These systems can indeed provide serious savings. A case study published by the DoE on an apartment complex in New York found that its geothermal heat pumps helped reduce energy costs by 40.7% across the 72-unit site.
Opened back in 2016, residents have seen average annual cost savings of approximately $24,000 per year, by now reaching a staggering quarter-million dollars in savings.
To that end, Vermont Gas has partnered with geothermal developer Dandelion Energy to install super efficient geothermal heating and cooling to the 44-unit Riggs Meadow affordable housing development in Hinesburg.
Drilling down into heated pockets of water below the Earth will begin in early 2027, while residents will be able to move in by year’s end.
The more high-profile geothermal installations in the US typically power large infrastructure, like Fervo Energy’s Corsac Station that ultimately serves Google-owned data centers. Yet others see the technology as ideal for utilities in modest-income housing.
In Detroit’s Virginia Park, the 27-unit Merrill Place II housing development for low and middle-income earners was designed with a geothermal heating and cooling system that, according to a release from the Mayor’s office , will make these utilities “free.”
“Our tenants are not billed separately for heating and cooling, which removes one of the most unpredictable and burdensome household expenses,” explained Sauda Ahmad-Green, lead developer on the project.
“That stability matters. It allows families to plan, to breathe a little easier, and to focus on building their futures instead of worrying about utility spikes.”
According to Dandelion Energy’s CEO Dan Yates, the Riggs Meadow development will be the first in the country where a utility—in this case natural gas—will directly own the geothermal installations, which they will operate as if they were gas lines.

items.text:
17 years ago today, Utah Jazz coach Jerry Sloan became the first in professional basketball history to win 1,000 games with a single team. Described as “one of the greatest and most respected coaches in NBA history,” he spent nearly his entire 23-year coaching career at Utah, managing the team through good times and bad, leading some spectacular talent such as Carlos Boozer and Karl Malone, and making the Western Conference playoffs 16 times in a row. READ excerpts from his milestone victory… (2009)
“Winning’s fine,” Sloan said, after the match, “but that’s a short-lived thing. Losing sticks with you for a long time.”
The victory of 104 to 97 over Oklahoma City meant Sloan’s record was 1,000 to 596, an average of 50 wins a season, or a nearly bang on 60% win rate, an impressive feat considering the grind of the NBA. In fact, he was one of three coaches in NBA history at the time to win 50 or more games on 10 separate occasions.
Under him, the Jazz had only one losing season in the past 20 by 2009. His teams made the playoffs 18 times, and he took them to 16 straight winning seasons (1988-2004), the second-longest streak in league history.
Happy Birthday to Joni Mitchell who turns 82 today. The Canadian singer-songwriter and painter is one of the most influential female musicians of the late 20th century. Her many hit songs include ” Both Sides Now ,” “ Chelsea Morning ,” “ Big Yellow Taxi, ” “ A Case of You ,” “ River, ” “ California, ” and “ Free Man in Paris ”—all recorded before she was 32.
Her distinctive open-tuned guitar was prompted by her childhood bout with polio which afflicted her fingers. Joni said the improvised tuning freed her songwriting, and was “a tool to break free of standard approaches to harmony and structure”.
Five years ago she suffered a brain aneurysm and she also suffers from a rare disorder called Morgellons disease. In recent years she channeled her creativity into a book of drawings and writings, Morning Glory on the Vine: Early Songs and Drawings , and a biography about her life, Reckless Daughter , which was released in 2017. (1944)

items.title: Venomous Primate Believed Extinct for 100 Years Was Hiding in Plain Sight All Along
items.desc: This big-eyed furball is the Bangka slow loris, a creature that in 2015 was believed to potentially be extinct. As the video demonstrates, the Bangka slow loris (N. bancanus) is still very much with us—thanks to a local wildlife organization on the island of Bangka that had been rescuing and returning them to the wild […] The post Venomous Primate Believed Extinct for 100 Years Was Hiding in Plain
items.text:
This big-eyed furball is the Bangka slow loris, a creature that in 2015 was believed to potentially be extinct.
As the video demonstrates, the Bangka slow loris ( N. bancanus) is still very much with us—thanks to a local wildlife organization on the island of Bangka that had been rescuing and returning them to the wild for years.
The last documented sighting of a Bangka slow loris in Western science occurred in the 1930s, and in 2015 it was considered “possibly extinct.” The organization’s years of work protecting these animals seems to have gone completely under the radar.
A paper published by Austrian scientists with international colleagues on the “rediscovery” details how their first notion that this species of slow loris still existed was a 2022 field guide to the primates of Indonesia.
The author, named Supriatna, mentioned the Gunung Maras National Park, a small forest near the city of Muntok on Bangka Island, as a habitat of the species.
Supriatna also cited another scientist’s unpublished thesis concerning Bangka slow lorises held at the Alobi Wildlife Rescue Center. From there it was a rather straightforward task of learning a bit more about the Alobi Center to determine that the animal had never gone extinct.
“By presenting the data collected by the Alobi Wildlife Rescue Center on N. bancanus since 2015, we demonstrate that the Bangka Slow Loris still exists and is probably more widely distributed across Bangka Island than previously documented,” the authors wrote.
Between 2015 and 2025, the center rescued more than 90 Bangka slow lorises, 86 of which were subsequently released, Smithsonian Magazine wrote . In almost all cases, the rescues were necessary because the animals had strayed too close to civilization and ended up in people’s gardens, plantations, or on roads.
The study is “another reminder that conservation depends on the knowledge of local communities, Indigenous peoples and others who know these species and landscapes intimately,” wrote Benji Barca, program manager for the global conservation organization Re:wild, in a statement. “A species can disappear from the scientific record without disappearing from the lives of the people who share its home.”
The Bangka slow loris is one of the world’s only venomous primates. Though omnivorous, this slow loris can secrete a toxin from glands located on its upper arms which it will lick and mix with its saliva to transform its defensive bite into a cytotoxic surprise.

Since then, she has become one of the most celebrated contemporary photographers around the world. Now, Iturbide’s work returns to SFMOMA with a retrospec
items.text:
Graciela Iturbide, ‘Mujer ángel, desierto de Sonora, México' (Angel Woman, Sonora Desert, Mexico), 1979; San Francisco Museum of Modern Art, purchase through a gift of Jane Reed and the Accessions Committee Fund © Graciela Iturbide
In 1990, the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art (SFMOMA) became the first American museum to give Mexican photographer Graciela Iturbide a monographic exhibition. Since then, she has become one of the most celebrated contemporary photographers around the world. Now, Iturbide’s work returns to SFMOMA with a retrospective spanning more than five decades of work.
Graciela Iturbide: Between Two Worlds features over 150 photographs taken between the 1960s and the 2010s, from her earliest experiments behind the camera as a young student to trips she took abroad later in life. Working almost exclusively in black and white, Iturbide’s photographs seem to exist at the intersection between life and death, tradition and mysticism, and reality and magic.
While some of her photographic series chronicle her journeys through places like the Southern U.S. and India, the bulk of Iturbide’s work paints an eerie yet soulful portrait of her home country. This can look like the busy markets in her hometown of Mexico City to religious rituals in Juchitán, a city in the southern state of Oaxaca with a large Zapotec population. “The camera is an excuse to share the life of the people, the rhythm and sympathy of festivals, to discover my country,” Iturbide says.
The exhibit also features some of the most famous pictures in Iturbide’s portfolio, such as Our Lady of the Iguanas, Juchitán, Oaxaca, Mexico . The striking portrait depicts a woman selling live iguanas, which she carries around on her head. To some, the image mirrors that of Medusa, with iguanas in place of snakes atop her head. Others draw a parallel between the iguanas and Christ’s crown of thorns, all while capturing the strong, defying look in her eyes.
“Graciela Iturbide’s photographs describe an array of life in Mexico that is so intimate and full of wonder that the viewer feels transported into a literary realm, like that of a vivid novel,” says Delphine Sims, assistant curator in the Department of Photography at SFMOMA.
Graciela Iturbide: Between Two Worlds will be on view through November 29, 2026. To plan your visit, learn more at SFMOMA’s website , and stay up to date by following SFMOMA on Instagram .

items.text:
Juchitán, Oaxaca, Mexico 1986 © Graciela Iturbide/Leica Hall of Fame Award 2026, Leica Gallery Wetzlar 2026
Mexican photographer Graciela Iturbide is celebrated among the creative community for her enigmatic yet eye-catching visual language. Her unique blend of mysticism, tradition, and identity, mostly shot in black and white, has earned Iturbide a place among the upper echelons of contemporary photography. Now, in recognition of her life’s work, Iturbide has been inducted into the Leica Hall of Fame.
The photographic equipment company has commended Iturbide’s oeuvre as, “Iconic images that have become etched into the collective memory are a testament to their work, touching the viewer and illustrating the ‘conditio humana’ in a timeless manner.” Iturbide is the first Latin American photographer to receive this honor, joining other legendary creatives like Steve McCurry, Joel Meyerowitz, Walter Vogel, Barbara Klemm, and Nick Út.
Born in Mexico City in 1942, Iturbide was immersed in photography from a young age, as her father was a devoted amateur photographer. She also surrounded herself with some of the most innovative creatives in her home country, working as an assistant to photographer Manuel Álvarez Bravo for a year. The death of her six-year-old daughter Claudia had a profound effect on her, prompting her to pursue a career as a professional photographer. In 1975, at age 33, she celebrated her first photographic exhibit in her hometown, and opened her first New York show the following year.
For the photographer, a picture’s quality has less to do with composition and more with what it can awaken in the viewer. “Difficult to say what a good photograph is made of. But for me, a good picture is the one that makes the other person feel something,” Iturbide says. In addition to the Leica Hall of Fame Award, Iturbide’s photograph Na’ Lupe Pan , taken in the southern state of Oaxaca in 1986, has been named Leica Picture of the Year 2026.
To showcase her work, Leica is celebrating an accompanying exhibition at the Leica Gallery in Wetzlar, Germany. Featuring over 50 photographs, the pictures include works from five different series. items.desc: Sniffer dogs are being trained in Germany to detect potentially destructive invasive plants—alien species that are one of the main causes of biodiversity loss worldwide. Scientists from Leipzig evaluated whether volunteer handlers and their dogs could be trained as effective detectives, and found the teams could locate invasive species in the wild with 75% accuracy. […] The post Dogs Can Sniff-Out
items.text:
Sniffer dogs are being trained in Germany to detect potentially destructive invasive plants—alien species that are one of the main causes of biodiversity loss worldwide.
Scientists from Leipzig evaluated whether volunteer handlers and their dogs could be trained as effective detectives, and found the teams could locate invasive species in the wild with 75% accuracy.
Other methods to combat invasive species have been costly and time-consuming, and the lack of effective early-detection methods has limited ecologists’ ability to control further colonization by invasive species.
Dr. Annegret Grimm-Seyfarth and her colleagues at the Helmholtz Centre for Environmental Research (UFZ) tested the feasibility of a volunteer dog-handler training program, so citizen scientists could join the fight.
31 dogs and their owners were trained between 2021 and 2023 using three highly problematic invasive plant species: Himalayan balsam, common ragweed, and those in the knotweed family, such as Japanese knotweed ( Fallopia spp. complex, Impatiens glandulifera, and Ambrosia artemisiifolia ).
The training culminated with a field test of the dogs’ ability to locate target species in the wild. Of the 12 teams that completed the field test, 11 teams passed, with an average detection success rate of 75%.
From the feasibility study, published in the journal PLOS One, the research team developed a set of recommendations to improve effectiveness of future, similar projects to improve volunteer selection and coordination, dog training, and initial deployments.
“Our study shows that trained volunteer dog-handler teams have real potential to support the early detection of invasive plants,” said Dr. Grimm-Seyfarth , in a media release.
“What we find particularly exciting is the opportunity to turn something people already love doing—spending time outdoors with their dogs—into a meaningful contribution to biodiversity conservation.”
“By combining dogs’ remarkable sense of smell with the enthusiasm of citizen scientists, we could expand monitoring efforts.
“With the right training, everyday walks could become an additional resource for detecting invasive plants early.”
Reliable monitoring requires more than a good nose, though. Training and continued guidance from both dog-training and ecological experts are needed to help volunteer teams succeed in real deployments.
Dogs have also been trained to sniff out invasive animals—like the notorious spotted lanternfly.

items.title: Seabirds See Miracle Recovery After Avian Flu Wiped Them Out
items.desc: Thanks to dedicated conservation efforts, sandwich terns have reclaimed a colony England’s south coast 3 years after they were wiped out by avian flu. Today, in what seems like a miracle, the birds have multiplied from 0 to 756. In addition to the sandwich terns, little terns, ringed plovers, black-headed gulls, and oystercatchers have all […] The post Seabirds See Miracle Recovery After Avian Flu
items.text:
Thanks to dedicated conservation efforts, sandwich terns have reclaimed a colony England’s south coast 3 years after they were wiped out by avian flu.
Today, in what seems like a miracle, the birds have multiplied from 0 to 756.
In addition to the sandwich terns, little terns, ringed plovers, black-headed gulls, and oystercatchers have all increased in number thanks to the same conservation work from the Royal Society for the Protection of Birds that helped encourage the sandwich terns to repopulate the area.
“In 2022, sandwich terns, black-headed gulls, and Mediterranean gulls were hit severely by HPAI/bird flu, leading to the abandonment of their breeding colony at Pagham harbor,” said Wez Smith, senior project manager for the RSPB .
“It’s taken several years of dedicated conservation action, but the situation began to ‘tern’ around last year, and the site is now thriving with record-breaking populations using it.”
Located between Brighton and Southampton on Britain’s Channel coastline, the Pagham colony was only the keystone in a 128,000-acre stretch of coastal habitat that has been the focus of conservation efforts by RSPB and other volunteers.
The Guardian reported that such efforts involve the establishment of predator-proof fencing to protect ground-nesting birds, monitoring for the presence of rats, and the selective removal of vegetation to encourage nesting behavior.
BRITISH BIRDLIFE: First Puffin Chick in 30 Years Spotted Emerging From Cliffs Along England’s South Coast
“Volunteers and rangers have also carried out patrols to raise awareness among visitors and local people of the vulnerability of ground-nesting birds to disturbance, with dog-friendly exercise areas provided away from the nesting birds,” the outlet added.
All of these areas and exercises are part of the Solent Seascape project —which works to restore multiple habitats across the Solent, a diverse estuarine system between the Isle of Wight and mainland England.

The exhibition transforms the gallery’s Nave into an immersive landscape filled with vivid color and shifting viewpoints. The artist draws on diverse
items.text:
Christian Achenbach, “Echotropia,” KÖNIG GALERIE, Berlin, 2026 © Christian Achenbach. (Photo: Roman März, courtesy of KÖNIG GALERIE)
At its St. Agnes space in Berlin, KÖNIG GALERIE presents ECHOTROPIA , an exhibition of new paintings by German artist Christian Achenbach . The exhibition transforms the gallery’s Nave into an immersive landscape filled with vivid color and shifting viewpoints. The artist draws on diverse art historical traditions to create imagined environments that move between abstraction and recognizable natural forms.
At the center of the exhibition, GENESIS commands attention with its expansive scale. Created specifically for the Nave, the painting measures approximately 8 meters (26.2 feet) wide and 3.6 meters (11.8 feet) tall. Its composition unfolds through wavy bands of color that ripple across the canvas. Rather than depicting a particular place, Achenbach uses color to establish its own rhythm and atmosphere.
An abstract grid occupies the foreground, recalling the enlargement techniques Renaissance painters used to transfer preliminary drawings onto larger surfaces. Its geometric structure contrasts with the expansive scenery behind it. Achenbach further disrupts conventional perspective by presenting multiple viewpoints within a single composition. The result recalls the concept of an “angle of totality” described by Chinese landscape painter Guo Xi, in which a landscape is understood through several vantage points rather than one fixed perspective.
Alongside the expansive landscapes, Achenbach introduces still lifes featuring floral arrangements positioned near windows and on terraces. Framed by elaborate curtains, the compositions suggest a quiet exchange between domestic interiors and the natural world beyond them. The flowers appear almost continuous with the surrounding landscape, softening the distinction between the two spaces.
Throughout the exhibition, Achenbach draws on diverse pictorial traditions, particularly Cubism and Fauvism . The former informs his fragmented spaces and shifting viewpoints, while the latter finds expression in his vivid use of color. Neither influence dominates. Instead, they intersect within compositions that move between recognizable landscapes and abstraction.

items.title: She Kept His Coat for 30 Years, Then Finally Found the Boy Who Gave It to Her After Racial Attack
items.desc: A coat once placed over the shoulders of a young girl whose traditional Korean uniform had been slashed in a racial incident 30 years ago has now been returned to the ‘good Samaritan’ who offered it. Norihisa Koyama was a Japanese high school student at the time of the notorious “hanbok slashing incidents” when he […] The post She Kept His Coat for 30 Years, Then Finally Found the Boy Who Gave It
items.text:
A coat once placed over the shoulders of a young girl whose traditional Korean uniform had been slashed in a racial incident 30 years ago has now been returned to the ‘good Samaritan’ who offered it.
Norihisa Koyama was a Japanese high school student at the time of the notorious “hanbok slashing incidents” when he saw a girl whose clothes were torn.
“A female student was crouching down and crying. I knew something was seriously wrong.”
The teen then gave her his brand new winter coat, just bought for him by his parents, to the Korean school student whose hanbok jacket (the traditional national attire of Korea) had been intentionally sliced open in public with a knife or scissors.
After he handed her his coat so she could cover herself and return home safely, he didn’t think much of it, but the girl carefully preserved the coat, which had his full name written on it, and never forgot his kindness.
Earlier this year, after three decades, the young woman was able to return the cherished black coat to Mr. Koyama, when she saw a newspaper article about his charity work and recognized his name.
Now age 50, he works with a Japanese nonprofit that supports single mothers and disadvantaged families
Mr. Koyama’s willingness to help others during his student days, seems to have been a precursor to his life’s work supporting single-parent and struggling families. Since the incident, he also has fostered close relationships with Korean residents in Japan.
In the 1980s and 1990s, there were dozens of occurrence of verbal abuse, assault, and injury against female middle and high school students of Korean schools who wore the traditional Korean dress (chima jeogori) as their uniform.
A Korean artist who resides in Japan painted a canvas at the time based on the “Chima Chogori slashing incidents” targeting ethnic Korean students in Japan during a time of military flare-ups involving N. Korea (much like the prejudice against Japanese-Americans during World War II).
It was an attempt to reinterpret the torn garment not as a memory of the suffering, but as an effort to mend and move on from the wounds he memorialized.
The artist, Park Chung-moon, heard about the reunion and invited Koyama to his Tokyo office in June to commemorate the return of the coat. He brought the wool garment to their meeting and together they spoke about the 1990s painting, and a new art project based on their inspiring story.

At Nightingale Gallery in Melbourne, Australia, a group exhibition titled A Certain Slant of Light brought together seven artists who celebrate nature in their own distin
items.text:
I just want to be in a place like this by Steen Foege
Landscape painting has appealed to artists since ancient times, and contemporary creatives continue to capture nature’s beauty with paint. At Nightingale Gallery in Melbourne, Australia, a group exhibition titled A Certain Slant of Light brought together seven artists who celebrate nature in their own distinct styles.
The show featured paintings by Angeline Bartholomeusz , Sharman Feinberg , Steen Foege , Suzanne Ganjineh , Jon Hewitt , Wendy Jagger , and Jessica Olpp . All seven artists draw inspiration from the natural landscapes around them, but each offers a unique perspective, capturing nature’s light, color, texture, and atmosphere in different ways.
Oil painter Jessica Olpp is known for her serene, often muted depictions of clouds drifting over open fields. She began painting as a meditative counterbalance to her career as a French teacher, and describes her work as reflecting “a quiet lyricism and deep appreciation for stillness.” Jon Hewitt and Steen Foege are also inspired by clouds. They bring stunning color to their sky paintings, using soft pastels and bold, vivid hues. Their work captures the magic of a changing sky, especially when clouds light up in shades of pink at sunrise and sunset.
Meanwhile, Sharman Feinberg’s colorful work captures the everyday life in her neighborhood, where parkland and rows of houses sit side by side. Wendy Jagger creates expressive, textured depictions of coastlines, and Angeline Bartholomeusz creates stunning tree paintings inspired by multiple horizons. Last but not least, Suzanne Ganjineh uses watercolor to paint her stunning scenes on linen.

items.text:
61 years ago today, the ironically-named Murder Act of 1965 is given Royal Assent, formally abolishing the death penalty in the United Kingdom for almost all crimes. Introduced by MP for Liverpool Sydney Silverman, it replaced hanging with mandatory sentences of life-imprisonment in all but 4 cases. The outstanding exceptions related to military-intelligence crimes, such as piracy with the intent to cause grievous injury, high treason, and espionage. READ more… (1965)
No executions have occurred in the United Kingdom since the Murder Act of 1965. The last were on August 13th, 1964, when Peter Allen and Gwynne Evans were hanged for murdering John Alan West during a theft four months earlier.
During the Troubles Westminster passed the Northern Ireland Constitution Act 1973, abolishing Stormont, and the Northern Ireland (Emergency Provisions) Act 1973, abolishing the death penalty for murder there. The death penalty was not fully abolished in the United Kingdom until 1998 by the Human Rights Act 1998 and the Crime and Disorder Act 1998.
735 years ago today, the Republic of Venice passed a law confining the city’s growing glassmaking industry to the island of Murano , giving birth to the tradition of Murano glass, one of the city’s most iconic characteristics. In the following century, exports began, and the island became famous, initially for glass beads and mirrors. Aventurine glass was invented on the island, and for a while Murano was the main producer of glass in Europe. Today, it’s a craft that is entering the fine art world.
From practical items like cups, bowls, lamps, and chandeliers, Murano artisans gradually began turning from applied art to fine art, with chandeliers becoming works of sculpture, and works of sculpture becoming masterpieces.
While the glass itself is delicate and dainty, a Murano glass artisan must be physically durable and resilient. Once he or she starts a piece, they cannot stop until it’s finished even if that means 16 hours of work. Neither the artisan, nor the glass can be allowed to cool down too much from the incredible heat of the furnaces, otherwise, the molten glass won’t be shapable anymore.
Murano glass artwork is now a more sensible business model for these artisans, as the high cost they merit is more flexible and can absorb higher energy prices in Europe as natural gas is needed to heat the furnaces.

items.text:
An English mayor-turned-detective solved the case of a thief who was looting $9,000 worth of historic capstones from a 300-year-old stone village wall—and he used a hi-tech tracker and a little trickery.
Around 30 stones went missing over a period of months from an 18th-century wall along a half-mile stretch of road leading into Rufford, Lancashire.
Lancashire Police said they were unable to help as the area had no CCTV coverage or “forensic opportunities”.
So Councillor Matt Smith and other locals decided to take matters into their own hands.
Instead of tolerating the loss, he placed an Apple AirTag inside one of the remaining stones which was already loose, hoping it would be stolen, with the GPS tracker revealing the perpetrator’s location.
“The audacity of him to steal from the community for his own personal gain,” said the 43-year-old local official. “That isn’t what we stand for.”
Worried locals noticed the wall was first attacked and stones were taken in May, with two further raids taking place in June and October.
Matt and other residents first put up signs saying “Smile, you’re on camera”, but that didn’t deter the criminal. They also thought about installing their own CCTV cameras, but it was “too expensive” for the small hamlet.
After the third attack in early October, Matt, who’s also a landscaping contractor ( M.Smith Gardens & Landscapes ), planted the tracker.
Within weeks, he woke up to find notifications on his phone revealing the stone had been moved overnight. He then contacted the police, passing on the whereabouts.
After the stones were found in his backyard, a 41-year-old Manchester man was arrested and sentenced.
On the scene police found a substantial number of coping stones from the vandalized wall, reportedly worth around £7,000 / $9,300—but Matt claims dozens of others were also found from across the country, making the estimated total value of up to £40,000.
Matt said it was very satisfying that the man was “brought to justice”, and the community’s effort was well “worth it”.

The curlew, mountain bumblebee, lapwing, and other wading birds are just some of the animals calling a one-of-a-kind noble estate home.
Now, people around the world have come together to donate millions to buy this critical piece of biodiverse land which had been in the hands of a British noble family for 800 years.
Sir David Attenborough celebrated the achievement, saying that “together, we’ve achieved something amazing.”
Attenborough is referring to the Rothbury Estate in Northumberland, described by the UK’s Wildlife Trusts as “a place of rare beauty… rolling moorlands, woodlands, and wide-open starry skies.”
Owned since the 13th century by the Dukes of Northumberland, it was recently acquired by the Wildlife Trusts following a remarkable funding call that saw £30 million be donated from over 25,000 supporters from 50 countries.
The plan for the estate, which covers 9,400 acres of the Scottish-English border, is to incorporate it into a 40-mile nature corridor across Northern England, stretching from Druridge Bay on the coastline to the east to an existing nature reserve to the west, and the estate, which had divided this key “moor to mar” ecosystem, right in the middle.
The curlew, mountain bumblebee, lapwing, and other wading birds live along the estate’s moors, while the woods provide a refuge for endangered red squirrels, cuckoos, and the UK’s smallest falcon, the merlin. A Critically-Endangered species of eel lives in the estate’s rivers along with salmon, while a variety of other songbirds, like the skylark, fly overhead.
“With the communities who live and work on and around the estate, we are developing a vision for the future management of this remarkable landscape,” the Wildlife Trusts wrote on their website .

Multiple partners, including the UK’s National Lottery Heritage Fund, the Department for Environment, Food, and Rural Affairs (DEFRA), and the Esmée Fairburn Foundation contributed to the fundraiser which was launched 2 years ago.

items.title: Was the British King Who Urged the Romans to Invade Actually a Queen? One Archaeologist Thinks So
items.desc: Linguistic clues and ancient coins could suggest that Verica—a ruler who fled Britain and convinced Roman Emperor Claudius to launch an invasion across the English Channel—has been misgendered for centuries
items.text:
In 43 C.E., the Roman Emperor Claudius invaded Britain, leading to its transformation it into an imperial province for nearly 400 years. This invasion was launched at the behest of an ousted British king named Verica, who fled across the English Channel to seek Roman aid. Now, a British archaeologist suggests that Verica was no king at all, but rather a queen.
The reassessment by Miles Russell , an archaeologist at Bournemouth University, reinterprets one of the most consequential figures of the late British Iron Age . Writing in Current Archaeology , Russell argues that “the assumption that this powerful ruler must have been male reflects a degree of unconscious bias, and perhaps a hangover from the patriarchal mindset of early Classicists.”
Verica was a Roman ally who led the Atrebates , a tribe whose territory spanned modern-day Berkshire, Hampshire and West Sussex. Around 40 C.E., during territorial upheavals following the death of powerful tribal leader Cunobelinus and the ascent of his son Caratacus , Verica was deposed and fled to Rome.
Roman historian Cassius Dio , writing in the early third century C.E., recorded that a Briton called “Berikos,” or “Bericus,” appealed directly to Claudius, handing the emperor a pretext for invasion. Without this appeal, “it’s likely that Rome would never have invaded,” Russell tells Gizmodo ’s Ed Cara.
He adds: “Verica was a major player in the story of how Britain became a Roman province and has been discussed in many books, papers and articles, but has always been misgendered.”
The first evidence that Russell presents to support the female identification is linguistic. In Iron Age Britain, personal names terminating in “-a” were overwhelmingly feminine. Two of the most prominent female British rulers— Boudica of the Iceni and Cartimandua of the Brigantes —both share this naming convention. Male names, on the other hand, tended to end with “os” or “us,” such as Cunobelinus. “It’s not a clear-cut rule,” but it applies to “about 95 percent of Iron Age British names,” Russell tells New Scientist ’s Michael Marshall.
Numismatic evidence also presents a striking departure from standard Iron Age coinage. While contemporary male leaders like Cunobelinus decorated their currency with overtly masculine warriors, coins struck under Verica depict “slender, bare-breasted equestrian figures that appear irrefutably female,” Russell writes.

items.text:
A man in southern Brazil was surprised to find a wad of cash on the ground in a public plaza with no one around looking for it.
Pedro Moro didn’t know it at the time, but he was holding a young construction worker’s entire monthly salary, which he had withdrawn from the bank in order to pay for the needs of his daughter.
Maybe Moro was inspired by the gigantic statue of Lord Buddha in the city, but he felt compelled to ensure the money was returned to its rightful owner.
Moro wrote to GNN that he found around US$219 worth of Brazilian reais in the plaza on August 28th in the city of Ibiraçu.
24-year-old Matheus Reginaldo Celestino was crossing the square on his way to a barbeque, but only realized the money was gone after he’d arrived.
Meanwhile, Moro found the money and waited to see if anyone came back looking for it. When nobody did, he took the money home and began posting on social media and other community channels asking if anyone had lost the money.
By September 3rd, no one had claimed it, so Moro returned to the plaza to visit local businesses and see if anyone had security camera footage of the moment the money had fallen there.
One such business had excellent footage in which Moro was able to see who dropped the money, which he shared again through socials asking if anyone knew the young man’s identity.
By then, Moro’s efforts had created quite the buzz in town.
“Everywhere I went [people would say] ‘Pedro, where’s the owner? Pedro, where’s the owner?’ I’m happy that I found the person and that I fulfilled my duty to return the money,” Moro told the Brazilian media outlet UOL.
Eventually, Celestino saw the post on Instagram and reached out to Moro, who in turn concluded a quick identity check, by asking him how many 10s, 20s, and 100s there were in the stack of cash.
“I had already taken that money for lost. But, thank God, everything worked out,” Celestino also told UOL.

items.text:
71 years ago, the Vienna State Opera reopened having been destroyed during World War II. Few cities have contributed more to classical music than the capital of Austria, and the State Opera hall has sourced many musicians to the Vienna Philharmonic orchestra, and hosted Gustav Mahler as its artistic director for many years. READ more about its design, destruction, and rebirth… (1955)
The State Opera was built in the Neo-Renaissance style by the Czech architect and contractor Josef Hlávka. A monumental demand for various kinds of fine stone existed in the Austro-Hungarian Empire at the time, so three different kinds were used. The public didn’t like the building at all.
In March 1945, the opera was set alight by an American bombardment. The auditorium and stage were destroyed by flames, as well as almost the entire décor and props for more than 120 operas with around 150,000 costumes. The front section, which had been walled off as a precaution, however, remained intact including the foyer, with frescoes by Moritz von Schwind, the main stairways, the vestibule and the tea room.
Lengthy discussion took place about whether the opera house should be restored to its original state on its original site, or whether it should be completely demolished and rebuilt, either on the same location or on a different site. It was rebuilt largely according to the original, unpopular design, but with modern improvements and finishings to reflect the stye of the day including new wooden flooring to help with acoustics. It opened with a performance of Beethoven’s Fidelio, the only opera the great composer ever wrote.
557 years ago, Guru Nanak, the spiritual teacher and founder of Sikhism, was born. A poet, mystic, philosopher, and singer, Guru Nanak ’s philosophy centered on belief in one God for all of creation, a God that is formless, omnipresent, compassionate, and attainable through prayer, humility, service, meditation, and virtuous living.
Nanak was born in Punjab, an area of Northern India and Pakistan. After a revelatory experience at the age of 37, Nanak traveled extensively to spread his message, that there is one God and one human race. He denounced ritualism, discrimination against women—and against those of lower socioeconomic status. This philosophy became the foundation of Sikhism (meaning: seeker or truth or disciple), which is today the fifth-largest religion in the world. (1469)

items.text:
A British adventurer who has walked around the world on a 28-year hike has finally reunited with his tearful mother.
Karl Bushby arrived back in his hometown of Hull after setting off on a 31,000-mile around-the-world trip in 1998 with the goal of returning home entirely on foot.
The media surrounded the former paratrooper for the emotional moment when he finally embraced his mom Angela at the gate of her home in England.
“28 years! I could not have imagined this,” said the 57-year-old.
“They say it takes a village, but it took a world to get me here—the kindness of strangers, so many, from individuals and nation states, to get me back here today.”
Pushing his cart, heavy with equipment like medicine, sleeping bags, and a spare tire, Karl was flanked by local well-wishers as he walked the final three miles home.
On his record-breaking walk, Karl braved the infamous Darien Gap, a stretch of dense rainforest and mountainous terrain in South America, was arrested in Russia, and swam across the Caspian Sea, to finally return home. ( See the video below, showing where he’s been… )
Karl was welcomed “like a modern folk hero” by local officials and hundreds of well-wishers on November 2 at Hull’s Queen Victoria Square, where he addressed the crowds:
“After 28 years, you couldn’t ask for more than this – this is the last few steps to my mother’s house.”
He originally hoped to reach Hull in 2012, but years of setbacks, including arrests in Russia and visa issues, meant he had to take breaks from his journey.
Earlier this year he was dealt another blow as he neared the finish line. He would be forced to face the prospect of swimming across the English Channel after being told he couldn’t use the Channel Tunnel to get from France to England.
GetLink, the operators of the tunnel, denied his formal request to walk through the service tunnel adjacent to the 31-mile long Channel Tunnel, saying (rather absurdly) that it would pose a safety risk if he were allowed to walk it.
According to Karl’s own rules, he cannot use any form of mechanized transport, including ferries.
Last year, Karl swam more than 170 miles across the Caspian Sea from Kazakhstan to Azerbaijan to avoid entering Iran or Russia.
It took him a whole month to swim and, looking ahead, he joked that he would rather consider taking hostages if it meant avoiding having to swim the Channel.
“I’m just not into the swim thing,” he said, especially because the English Channel is a wholly different stretch of water

items.text:
When it comes to choosing a restaurant, we all have our preferences, right, pandas? Some of us look for delicious food at reasonable prices, while others care more about the ambience, portion sizes, or service. But there's one thing most of us probably wouldn't want to compromise on: cleanliness. After all, even the tastiest meal can lose its appeal if the plates are dirty, the tables are sticky, or the toilets smell unpleasant!
Interestingly, a survey conducted by OnePoll on behalf of P&G Professional found that cleanliness was a top priority for American diners. The poll, which included 1,000 consumers and 1,000 business owners and hospitality workers, revealed that 44% of consumers prioritized cleanliness when choosing a restaurant, compared with 35% who valued menu variety and 33% who considered affordability important. And it's not just a minor preference.
The same survey found that 61% of Americans considered uncleanliness a dealbreaker at restaurants, while 62% felt the same way about hotels.
But let's talk about one particular part of a restaurant that can make or break the experience: the bathroom. You might have enjoyed a fantastic meal, but discovering a dirty restroom afterward could leave you with a completely different impression. In fact, a study published in the Journal of Foodservice found that restroom cleanliness plays an important role in how customers judge a restaurant's hygiene. It can even influence where they choose to eat and whether they decide to return.
To understand this better, Bored Panda spoke with Dr. Sumersing Patil and Pravin Kadam, co-owners of Swaad – Assal Marathi , a restaurant in Munich, Germany, serving authentic Maharashtrian cuisine.
"Of course, good food, friendly service, and a nice atmosphere matter. But you can't ignore the toilets! Think about it. Now, imagine they've had a lovely meal, but the toilet is dirty or smells bad. That's probably what they'll remember! And they might think twice before coming back. items.desc: Stained glass is something that most of us don’t get to see on a daily basis. Unless you’re frequenting cathedrals or creating pieces yourself, you’re probably not encountering very much stained glass. But maybe you should be! Here’s a list of some of the most creative and stunning stained glass pieces that artists have shared online.
items.text:
Stained glass is something that many of us love to admire when we encounter it but that most of us see very rarely. It’s also probably a style of artwork that you know very little about, so if you’re interested in finding out about the history of stained glass, we’ve got you covered. According to The Stained Glass Association of America , this style of artwork has actually been around for over a thousand years.
One of the earliest known examples of multicolored pieces of glass being used in a window was discovered at St. Paul’s Monastery in Jarrow, England, which was founded in 686 AD. Experts also believe that Arabian stained glass windows appeared during the second half of the 13th century.
Stained glass was never purely a Christian art form, but it is present in many Christian churches and cathedrals today. The style of this artwork has transformed over time. During the Romanesque period, the most predominant colors used were red and blue, and much of the artwork depicted well-known saints or stories from the Bible.
During the Gothic era, however, it was more common for stained glass to feature “symbolism based on bestiaries” or “unnatural history.” And depending on the location of the church, there may have been reds and blues or whites, yellows, and greens used in the artwork.
Once the Renaissance period began, stained glass started to look very different. One major difference was that stained glass started appearing in secular buildings as well. And the subjects featured in stained glass artwork were often dressed in period clothing, depicting historical scenes, allegorical themes, and figures representing abstract ideas. It also became more common for artists to ship their pieces across large distances, meaning that stained glass started popping up in more and more locations across Europe.
Today, stained glass can be used for much more than just church windows. As you can see from this list, there are plenty of creative artists out there who are pushing the boundaries of what can be made with stained glass. And if you’re interested in taking up this hobby yourself, Different Glass has some advice for beginners.
First, they note that this can be a great craft to take up if you’re looking for a creative outlet or a new technical challenge. It’ll provide you with the joy of creating something new, but it can also be an incredibly calming and healing hobby.

items.desc: A Tale of Two Bobs: Pope Leo XIV and Bob Dylan Meet up in the Vatican Embed from Getty Images As luck would have it, two of the most influential men in the world are both named Bob; one is a Nobel Prize winner, and the other happens to be the Pope. items.text:
As luck would have it, two of the most influential men in the world are both named Bob; one is a Nobel Prize winner, and the other happens to be the Pope. Now, the two figures have crossed paths in an encounter of massive proportions. Singer-songwriter Bob Dylan and Pope Leo XIV, whose birth name is Robert Prevost, recently met up in the Vatican.
The 85-year-old Dylan visited 71-year-old Prevost during a break between concert dates in Italy. The meeting, which was private, lasted about 10 minutes. The pair exchanged gifts during the get-together; the Pope presented Dylan a rosary, while the musician gifted the Pope a signed copy of his autobiography, Chronicles: Volume One , first published in 2004.
While they had previously never met in person, the pair had been in each other’s orbits. According to reports, Dylan had been wanting to speak with the Pope for some time. And Pope Leo quoted an unpublished protest song by Dylan in his recently published book Disarmed and Disarming: Peace Is a Gift . Titled “Go Away You Bomb,” the song features the message: “I hate you cause yer man-made and man-owned, an’ man-handled,” which Pope Leo borrowed to warn humanity about nuclear weapons.
The images of the encounter also made waves for Dylan’s choice of clothes. Over the last couple of years, the singer has performed in near darkness, often with a black hood pulled over his head to conceal his face from the audience. Dylan visited the Pope wearing that same moody outfit, creating a stark contrast with the Pope’s pristine white robes and cheerful smile.
The meeting was arranged by Rev. Antonio Spadaro, a Vatican official, writer, and editor who has tried to narrow the wide gap between the church and global culture. As such, Dylan’s visit follows a meeting between Pope Leo and Patti Smith earlier this year. This also happened to be the second time Dylan has met a pope. In 1997, he played for Pope John Paul II during a concert in Bologna, Italy.

items.text:
In a romantic landscape dominated by dating apps , Finland is presenting another option. The world’s happiest country is inviting 16 international singles on an all-expenses-paid trip that combines Finnish food, travel, and the possibility of making a romantic connection.
The Finnish Dinner Date is the latest part of Visit Finland’s Have Some Finnish campaign, which was created to introduce more travelers to the country’s relatively under-the-radar food culture. In February 2027, selected participants will travel to either Helsinki or Tampere for a four-day culinary experience that ends with a group blind date over one of Finland’s official tasting menus.
Eight international travelers will be selected for each destination, for a total of 16 winners. Each group will eventually sit down for dinner with two local Finnish singles, although romance isn’t exactly guaranteed. Visit Finland seems just as interested in helping participants fall for Finnish food and the country itself.
“Finnish food is a direct expression of our famously happy way of life: a way of connecting to place, to season, and to the people around you,” says Heli Jimenez, senior director of international marketing at Business Finland. “Food brings Finns together, and now we are inviting travelers to join us in a truly one-of-a-kind way.”
The four-day trips will take place February 9–19, 2027. Participants won’t even know whether they’ve been matched with Helsinki or Tampere until they are selected, making their destination the first surprise of the experience. Along with the dinner date itself, the trip includes a hosted itinerary filled with activities and meals.
The dating idea was partly inspired by a charming Finnish phenomenon known as the sinkkukori , or “single basket.” Some Finnish grocery stores offer pink shopping baskets that shoppers can carry to quietly signal that they’re single and open to meeting someone. After the idea gained attention online, Visit Finland decided to bring a similar spirit to its food campaign.
To be considered, applicants must create a video answering the question, “What would you serve on a dinner date, and why?” and post it to Instagram, TikTok, or YouTube with the campaign hashtag before completing an online application. Applications are open until November 10, 2026, at 11:59 a.m. Finnish time, and the selected participants are expected to be announced on December 1.

items.desc: A meteor shower famous for its fireballs will be visible around the world next week. Though the Northern Taurid Meteor Shower doesn’t peak until 3 days later, the best chance to catch its renowned shooting stars is Monday the 9th, when the New Moon guarantees the least amount of light pollution. That will be key […] The post Next Week’s New Moon Is Perfect Backdrop to Blazing Tails of Taurid Meteo
items.text:
A meteor shower famous for its fireballs will be visible around the world next week.
Though the Northern Taurid Meteor Shower doesn’t peak until 3 days later, the best chance to catch its renowned shooting stars is Monday the 9th, when the New Moon guarantees the least amount of light pollution.
That will be key to enjoying the N. Taurids and their famously long, luminescent tails that streak across the sky. This meteor shower produces around 8-12 shooting stars per hour.
Tuesday the 10th would be likely just as good a time, as a 1-day-old moon isn’t likely to create much of a glare.
If you’ve ever fancied trying celestial photography, the long Taurus tails make for excellent subject matter. Amateurs can simply place their camera’s mode setting on shutter priority and slow the speed down for a 20 or 30-second exposure.
Place the camera on a tripod with the widest field of view and aim it at the constellation of Taurus, where it will appear the meteors emanate from. Taurus is located just northeast of Orion and contains the Pleiades.
Again, the peak of the meteor shower will be closer to the 12th, so any night next week could well produce a great show.

items.text:
Studio Ghibli’s Little Humidifiers featuring Totoro, Jiji, and Calcifer in tiny scenes inspired by their respective films. (Photo: Benelic / Donguri Kyowakoku)
There’s never been a cuter way to ease the negative effects of dry air. Studio Ghibli specialty shop Donguri Kyowakoku in Japan has brought back its beloved Little Humidifiers for the season, featuring Calcifer from Howl’s Moving Castle , Totoro from My Neighbor Totoro , and Jiji from Kiki’s Delivery Service . The compact desktop humidifiers bring some Studio Ghibli magic to your home or workspace while helping combat dry fall and winter air.
The Totoro humidifier features both a big and small Totoro perched atop its water reservoir. The larger forest spirit plays his recognizable ocarina, with mist billowing directly from the instrument as though he’s really blowing into it. Nearby, the smaller Totoro holds up a flower, while a few tiny Soot Sprites hide inside the tree trunk.
Each humidifier stands around 22 centimeters (8.7 inches) tall, with a base roughly the size of a drink bottle or thermos. Their compact footprint makes them easy to fit beside a laptop, on a nightstand, or in another cozy corner of your home.
Calcifer from Howl’s Moving Castle is especially well-suited to the role of humidifier. The little fire demon is shown cooking the film’s memorable bacon-and-egg breakfast, with mist rising from beneath the frying pan on his back, creating the illusion of steam coming from the hot food.
Jiji’s design is equally clever. The black cat from Kiki’s Delivery Service sits beside a breakfast spread complete with pancakes and a red mug. Mist rises directly from the cup, making it look as though someone has just poured a fresh cup of coffee.
Beyond being adorable decorations, the humidifiers are designed for practical everyday use. Each one is powered by USB and comes with its own cable. A full reservoir provides approximately eight hours of continuous use, after which the device automatically shuts off.
Each humidifier is priced at ¥5,280 (about $33). The seasonal collection is currently available through Donguri Kyowakoku, giving fans of My Neighbor Totoro , Howl’s Moving Castle , and Kiki’s Delivery Service a particularly charming way to make the dry season a little more comfortable.

items.text:
Chonon Bensho, Jone Metsa Noma (The beautiful woman of the invisible jungle), 2022. Hand embroidery on cotton, 98 x 138 cm. Courtesy of the artist and W-galería.
Frieze is expanding its international art fair calendar with the inaugural edition of Frieze Abu Dhabi. Taking place at Manarat Al Saadiyat, the fair will bring together 89 exhibitors from 37 countries and regions. Its program connects artists from West Asia, North Africa, and South Asia with international voices, exploring the histories and cultural exchanges that have shaped the region.
The fair is organized into four sections: Galleries, Focus, Frieze Masters Abu Dhabi, and Global Futures. Together, they span contemporary and historical art, bringing different generations and artistic perspectives into conversation.
The main Galleries section features more than 60 galleries presenting work from the mid-20th century to today. Regional art histories take center stage alongside international practices. Presentations include works by pioneering Arab artists and contemporary voices exploring identity, social change, and cultural memory. Several galleries will also highlight artists from the UAE, reflecting the country’s evolving creative landscape.
Frieze’s Focus section will spotlight younger galleries through a series of experimental solo presentations. One highlight is the presentation by Dala Nasser at Commonwealth and Council. The inaugural Frieze Abu Dhabi Artist Award recipient will showcase works incorporating rubbings of ruins, tombs, and rock surfaces across Western Asia. Using ash and natural pigments, Nasser’s practice considers the relationship between landscape, history, and memory.
Meanwhile, Frieze Masters Abu Dhabi takes a step back in time. Curated by Marika Sardar, the section explores the Indian Ocean as a historic center of trade and cultural exchange. Rare books, manuscripts, maps, and artifacts will trace the movement of people, objects, and knowledge between West Asia, East Africa, and South Asia. Among the highlights is a first-century painted portrait known as Portrait L , which will be exhibited in the Middle East for the first time since leaving Egypt in 1888.
Global Futures, curated by Tarini Malik, brings together eight solo presentations exploring connections across generations and geographies. The artists consider themes of place, identity, and memory through works that draw on their cultural backgrounds and lived experiences.

items.text:
Inspired by how flowers open and close from day to night, Amsterdam-based experiential art duo Lonneke Gordijn and Ralph Nauta of Studio DRIFT created a series of site-specific kinetic installations that celebrate nature’s beauty and rhythms . Their mechanical flowers have been installed across Europe, and now they’ve arrived in Las Vegas, where Shy Society Palazzo transforms the Palazzo Lobby at The Venetian Resort .
The installation features nine Shylight sculptures and 18 Meadow sculptures, each opening, retreating, and moving in choreographed sequences. Throughout the day, the mesmerizing, suspended display shifts in a continuous flow. “Nature is a system in which everything is connected,” said Nauta. “By bringing Shylight and Meadow together, the individual becomes part of a larger collective movement. Shy Society Palazzo makes this connection visible, reminding us that we are not separate from nature, but part of it.”
Once every hour, the sculptures come together for a fully choreographed performance accompanied by music. The sequence is inspired by the rhythms of the human body, from our breathing and heartbeat to the movements of our nervous system, encouraging visitors to pause and reflect on the constant change happening within themselves.
“We created this experience to welcome our guests into a world of wonder from the moment they arrive,” said Marcy Miles, chief marketing officer of The Venetian Resort Las Vegas. “The Venetian Resort exists at the intersection of art, architecture and hospitality and Shy Society Palazzo is a stunning expression of that vision. This installation transforms a shared space into a cultural experience, inviting guests from around the world to engage with art in an unexpected and deeply personal way. Through movement, light, and responsiveness, the work celebrates curiosity, transformation, and the connections that unite us.”

items.text:
A pet budgie that vanished when a storm blew open a kitchen window was found hiding in a storm drain a mile from home.
Luna made her great escape from owner Cimberley Frost’s home in Northampton, England when strong winds following Storm Boelo forced open a window and she flew away.
But the tiny bird’s adventure didn’t end in disaster.
A passing motorist spotted her hopping down into a roadside drain and alerted the RSPCA.
“Luna hadn’t gone far when we believe she must have been frightened by something and she hopped down into a drain to hide,” said RSPCA Inspector Richard Durant.
“Luckily, in a bizarre turn of events, a passing driver happened to spot her jump down into the drain and called us for help.
Richard was out with Trainee Animal Rescue Officer Rosie Cowie on October 26 when the call came to rescue the stranded 11-month-old bird.
“We peered down the drain and there was Luna’s little beak peeking out from a pipe,” recalled Rosie.
“I gently grabbed her and popped her in a pet carrier—my first rescue, and one I certainly won’t be forgetting.”
Luna was taken into RSPCA care and, just days later, her worried owner got in touch.
RSPCA Officer Ellie Grindod reunited Luna with a relieved Ms. Frost, whose home was just a mile from where the budgie had been found.
“We left the window open hoping she might come back, and went out to try to find her. We played budgie noises to see if it would help her find her way home but nothing.”
Smartly, she posted on social media and then someone got in touch to say they’d heard the RSPCA had picked up a budgie nearby.
“The house was so quiet without her; she’s always squeaking and talking. We really missed her; now she’s back to being Lady of the house.”

Luna loves spending her days flying around the flat, taunting family dog Ziggy and demanding to be let out of her cage, or finding her own way out.
Now, with her reputation as an escape artist, the family will likely be more cautious.
“It’s her first adventure, and hopefully her last!”

items.text:
A baby’s life was likely saved after his racing heartbeat was detected by the family dog—that wouldn’t stop crying.
Kim Reynolds was confounded by her doberman’s unusual “needy” behavior around six-month-old Alexander.
Saraya wouldn’t leave the baby’s side and cried every time he was taken away from her that morning.
The boy later became upset and looked unwell, so his mom drove him to the hospital, where doctors discovered Alexander was suffering with a dangerously-fast heart rhythm—at 280 beats per minute.
“Saraya knew his heart rate was higher than it should’ve been.
“She sensed it,” said the 41-year-old mom. “I had no idea.”
“I dread to think what would have happened if I just put him in the cot and walked away.”
After two days in the hospital, he was diagnosed with Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome, which isn’t dangerous, if treated, but if left untreated can be deadly.
When she went to the hospital emergency room, Kim feared they were wasting professional’s time because the baby had stopped crying, but three doses of medication finally brought his heart rate down and the family was transferred by ambulance to another hospital.
“It was bugging me that Saraya was trying to tell me (that) something wasn’t right,” said the first-time-mom from Somerset, England.
“It certainly added to my concern, and made us go in to get checked.”
Now 9-months-old, the baby takes the beta blocker propranolol orally three times a day.
Kim said he “knows he needs it” and drinks from the syringe himself “hassle free”.
This month, the pooch Saraya began acting different around Alexander again.
“He was in his bouncer and she was next to him, licking his hands, looking at me.”
“My first thought was ‘oh god, are we going to go into SVT again?’’’
After checking his pulse, she noticed his throat looked red and took him to the hospital, where he was diagnosed with bacterial tonsillitis and prescribed penicillin.
“She’s not trained or a registered assistance dog but, every opportunity I have, she will be by his side.”
“It’s been a whole experience. It’s really important to raise awareness. You wonder how many babies have SVT and don’t realize.

items.text:
At a small store in Stockholm, there’s a discount if you pay with bad breath.
In fact, they’ll give you everything you need: toothpaste, a toothbrush, flossers, and more all for free—provided your breath is sufficiently rancid.
A post shared by The Humble Co. (@thehumble.co)
Jokes aside, the Swedish oral care company The Humble Co. commissioned a survey that found 1 in 3 people experience bad breath at least weekly, while 50% have avoided telling someone else their breath stinks.
To help clear the air, Humble Co. opened the Breath Boutique in the Hornstull neighborhood of Sweden.
“Your breath usually pays the price for a poor oral care routine. With this campaign, we turned that around and let people literally pay for a better one,” say Martin Noreby and Simon Lublin, creative directors behind the idea.
Anyone can come to the Breath Boutique and use a handheld analyzer to measure sulfur compounds in their breath.
Rated on a scale of 1 – 4, sufficiently stinky breath is an acceptable payment method for The Humble Company’s line of oral care products.
“By turning bad breath into a payment method, we wanted to make the subject less awkward, challenge the taboo, and inspire more people to take care of their oral health,” says Louise Lehmann, Marketing Manager at The Humble Co.
